claims.text: Controlled Nb addition induces Nb segregation at grain boundaries in Fe–Cr steels.
Nb grain-boundary segregation stabilizes the passive oxide film.
Stabilization of the passive oxide film by Nb enhances corrosion resistance.
High-alloy Fe–Cr steels naturally form passive oxide films.
Acidic chloride solutions at elevated temperatures replicate corrosive conditions typical of both chemical-processing and nuclear-power service.
Increasing Nb concentration at grain boundaries produces a more uniform passive film.
Increasing Nb concentration at grain boundaries produces a more defect-resistant passive film.
Nb grain-boundary segregation reduces the defect density of the passive film.
Nb grain-boundary segregation enhances the chemical stability of the passive film.
Reduced defect density and enhanced chemical stability mitigate localized passive-film breakdown.
Mitigation of localized passive-film breakdown lowers the corrosion rate relative to untreated Fe–Cr steel.
Nb-microalloyed steels will develop a thinner passive film than the untreated baseline.
Nb-microalloyed steels will develop a denser passive film than the untreated baseline.
Nb-microalloyed steels will develop a more homogeneous passive film than the untreated baseline.
Nb-microalloyed steels will show improved electrochemical impedance responses relative to the untreated baseline.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement can depend on alloy composition, processing parameters, and test conditions.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy can evaluate passive-film integrity and electrochemical behavior in this study.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can characterize passive-film composition and thickness in this study.
Scanning electron microscopy can assess whether the passive film is denser and more homogeneous.
Failure of Nb-microalloyed samples to show statistically significant passive-film and corrosion improvements relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
